notes.b: As a fat is heated it passes through three different stages, each at a higher temperature than the last: it melts, then it smokes, then it can burst into flame. Knowing these temperatures explains how fats are chosen and used in cooking.
points: Melting point is the temperature at which a solid fat turns to liquid. Fats are mixtures of triglycerides, so they melt over a range rather than at one sharp temperature, and solid fats melt at about 30–40 °C. Oils are already liquid at room temperature.

Fats with a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids have lower melting points, because their kinked chains do not pack tightly. Fats with more saturated fatty acids, whose chains are straight and pack closely, have higher melting points.
Smoke point is the temperature at which an overheated lipid begins to decompose and gives off a continuous blue haze. Smoke points are about 200 °C for solid fats and about 250 °C for oils.
On decomposition the fat splits into glycerol and fatty acids, and the glycerol breaks down further to release acrolein, which has an acrid, irritating smell.

Free fatty acids, impurities and food particles left in the oil lower its smoke point, and repeated use builds these up, so used or dirty fat smokes at a lower temperature. This is why frying fat is strained and replaced.
A fat with a high smoke point suits frying, while butter, with a lower smoke point, burns.
Flash point is the temperature at which the vapour from an overheated lipid ignites spontaneously and bursts into flame. Flash points are about 310 °C for solid fats and about 325 °C for oils.
A fat that reaches its flash point is a serious fire hazard. Never leave a deep-fat fryer unattended, never heat fat until it smokes, and smother a fat fire with a fire blanket or lid, never water.
notes.tip: Melting, smoke and flash points are three different temperatures in increasing order, and smoke is the warning stage before flash point. For each one you are asked to define, give the decomposition products (glycerol and fatty acids, acrolein, blue haze), the approximate temperature, the fire-hazard consequence, and that impurities lower them.

notes.h: Investigation: comparing melting, smoke and flash points
notes.b: This practical compares how common fats and oils behave on heating, and links the results to their fatty acids and to impurities. Care is needed because the fats become very hot.
points: Aim: to compare the melting, smoke and flash points of common fats and oils, for example butter, lard, olive oil and sunflower oil.
1. Use a small amount of each fat or oil, so any smoke or fire is limited.
2. Heat each gently, preferably on a hot plate rather than a flame, which is safer for a class demonstration, and read the temperature with a thermometer.
3. Record the order in which the fats melt, and which fats smoke first. Do not heat beyond the smoke point.
Conclusion: link the order of melting points to how saturated the fatty acids are, and the point at which smoke appears to the fat's impurities.

notes.b: Oil and water do not mix normally, but they can be forced to, and in some foods they stay mixed. This is the basis of mayonnaise, butter, milk and many sauces.
points: An emulsion is a mixture of two liquids that do not normally mix (immiscible), such as oil and water, with one dispersed as tiny droplets in the other.
Vigorous shaking, whisking or blending forces the liquids together by breaking one liquid into droplets that spread through the other.
A temporary emulsion, such as French dressing (oil and vinegar), separates again on standing because nothing keeps the droplets apart.
A permanent (stable) emulsion, such as mayonnaise, hollandaise sauce, ice cream, cream, milk or butter, stays mixed because an emulsifying agent coats the droplets.
An emulsifier has a hydrophilic (water-attracting) end and a hydrophobic (water-repelling) end, which sit at the boundary between the oil and the water.
In an oil-in-water emulsion, oil droplets are dispersed in water, as in mayonnaise, milk and cream.
In a water-in-oil emulsion, water droplets are dispersed in fat, as in butter, margarine and some spreads.
notes.tip: An emulsion is not a solution: oil and water do not dissolve, and droplets of one are suspended in the other. A full answer gives immiscible liquids forced together, temporary versus permanent with examples, the emulsifier's two ends, and oil-in-water versus water-in-oil.

notes.b: Making mayonnaise and a French dressing side by side shows the difference between a temporary and a permanent emulsion.
points: Aim: to show emulsion formation and the effect of an emulsifier, using mayonnaise (egg yolk, oil, and vinegar or lemon juice) and a French dressing (oil and vinegar).
1. Make the mayonnaise by adding the oil to the egg yolk slowly while whisking, so the droplets are small and evenly spread.
2. Shake the oil and vinegar together for the French dressing, and leave both to stand.
Result: the French dressing separates, but the mayonnaise stays stable because the egg yolk is the emulsifier. Comparing with and without an emulsifier shows this.

notes.h: Emulsifying agents and stabilisers (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Two kinds of additive help keep an emulsion together, and they do different jobs. An emulsifier makes the emulsion, while a stabiliser helps it stay that way.
points: An emulsifying agent is a molecule with a hydrophilic (water-loving) end and a hydrophobic (water-hating, fat-loving) end. The hydrophilic end attaches to the water and the hydrophobic end to the oil, so the droplets are coated and cannot join together.

Emulsifying agents include lecithin (found in egg yolk and soya; the food additive E322), mustard, and mono- and diglycerides such as glycerol monostearate (GMS; mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids are E471).
The function of an emulsifier is to reduce the tension between oil and water so they mix, and to make and keep the emulsion stable.
Stabilisers do not form the emulsion. They thicken the water phase and stop droplets joining together (coalescing).
Examples of stabilisers are starch, pectin, gelatine and gums such as xanthan gum and guar gum. They are used in dressings, sauces, ice cream and low-fat spreads.
notes.tip: Examiners expect you to separate the two: the emulsifier has the two ends and forms the emulsion, while the stabiliser thickens and prevents separation. Do not call mustard or lecithin a stabiliser.

notes.b: Some fats can be spread or shaped without being runny or rock hard. This property, called plasticity, is why butter and margarine behave so differently from oil.
points: Plasticity is the ability of a fat to be shaped, spread or worked (creamed, rubbed in) at a given temperature without being fully liquid or fully hard.

It is due to a mixture of solid and liquid fat within the fat: the solid fat forms a network that holds the liquid fat. The proportion of saturated fatty acids only decides how much of the fat is solid.

Butter, lard, margarine and shortening are plastic over a range of temperatures. Oils are not plastic, a very unsaturated fat is too liquid to hold its shape, and a very saturated fat is hard and brittle when cold.
Plastic fats are valued in pastry and cake making because they can be creamed, which traps air, or rubbed into flour and layered. Plasticity also gives butter and margarine their spreadability.
notes.tip: Exams pair plasticity with hydrogenation: say it is the ability to be spread or shaped, and name spreading and pastry or cake making as why it matters.

notes.b: Liquid oils can be turned into solid fats by changing their fatty acids. This process, hydrogenation, is how margarine is made from vegetable oils.
points: Hydrogenation is the addition of hydrogen to the double bonds of unsaturated fatty acids, using a nickel catalyst under heat and pressure.
It converts unsaturated fatty acids to saturated ones, so a liquid oil becomes a semi-solid or solid fat.
It is used to make margarine and spreads, hard margarines, shortenings and baking fats from liquid vegetable oils. The fats are solid, plastic and more stable against oxidative rancidity.
Partial hydrogenation forms trans fatty acids, so the process is now controlled. Full hydrogenation gives a hard saturated fat.
notes.tip: Hydrogenation turns oils into fats by adding hydrogen at the double bonds, not by adding water. The nickel is a catalyst and is not used up.

notes.b: Rancidity is the spoilage of fats and oils, which gives them an unpleasant taste and smell. It happens in two different ways, with different causes.
points: Oxidative rancidity: oxygen from the air reacts at the double bonds of unsaturated fatty acids, which also breaks the chain. This produces aldehydes and ketones, which cause the rancid smell.
Light, heat and traces of metal ions speed up oxidative rancidity. It affects polyunsaturated oils most because they have the most double bonds.

Hydrolytic rancidity: water, together with the enzyme lipase from the food itself or from micro-organisms such as moulds and bacteria, breaks fats down into fatty acids and glycerol. The free fatty acids, for example butyric acid in butter, give the smell.
Hydrolytic rancidity can occur in a freezer, because lipase is not destroyed by freezing. Blanching vegetables before freezing destroys these enzymes.

Fats are protected from rancidity when stored in airtight, opaque containers in a cool, dark place, kept dry, bought in small amounts and used before the date. Refrigerating or freezing, using less-unsaturated fats, adding antioxidants and not reusing frying oil repeatedly also help.
notes.tip: Oxidative rancidity needs oxygen and double bonds. Hydrolytic needs water and lipase and does not depend on double bonds, so saturated fats can go rancid this way too. Give the cause, the products and how to prevent each.

notes.b: Antioxidants are the main chemical defence against oxidative rancidity. They are added to fats and oils so that they keep their flavour for longer.
points: An antioxidant is a substance that slows oxidation. It delays oxidative rancidity by reacting with oxygen or free radicals before they attack the double bonds.
Natural antioxidants include vitamin E (tocopherols, E306), present in some vegetable oils, and vitamin C (ascorbic acid, E300).
Synthetic antioxidants added to fats include butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA, E320) and butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT, E321).

Antioxidants are added to oils, margarines, spreads, snack foods and fried foods to keep their flavour and extend their shelf life. They appear in the ingredients list by name or E number under the additives rules (Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008).
notes.tip: Name an antioxidant (vitamin E, vitamin C, BHA or BHT) and state its function: it delays oxidative rancidity, keeping flavour and increasing shelf life.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by the smoke point and the flash point of a fat, and state why a fat with a low smoke point is less suitable for deep-fat frying.
questions.model: Smoke point: the temperature at which a fat begins to decompose and give off a continuous blue haze. Flash point: the higher temperature at which the vapour from the overheated fat ignites spontaneously. A fat with a low smoke point starts to decompose at a lower temperature during frying, producing acrid smoke and acrolein, giving a poor flavour and a fire risk. Award one mark for each correct point, up to 6.

questions.prompt: Describe how an emulsion forms, and discuss the roles of emulsifying agents and stabilisers in keeping an emulsion stable, giving one permanent and one temporary example.
questions.model: Immiscible oil and water are forced together by vigorous shaking, whisking or blending, which breaks one liquid into droplets dispersed through the other. An emulsifying agent has a water-attracting end and a water-repelling end, so it sits at the boundary between oil and water and coats the droplets, preventing them from joining together. Lecithin in egg yolk and mustard are examples of emulsifying agents. Stabilisers such as starch or gums thicken the water phase, slowing the movement of droplets and keeping the emulsion stable. A permanent emulsion is mayonnaise, an oil-in-water emulsion held together by egg yolk lecithin. A temporary emulsion is French dressing, which separates on standing and must be shaken before use. A labelled diagram showing an emulsifier at the oil-water boundary may also be included.
